title: A Big Reason Why You May Be Struggling With Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a personality trait common among struggling teachers: caring too much. He argues that tying one's hopes and feelings too tightly to students' performance leads directly to micromanagement—over-helping, narrating, reminding, and constantly checking in—which stresses out teachers and, paradoxically, invites misbehavior. When teachers absorb too much emotional investment in outcomes, students are left with no room to care about their own learning or behavior, so they disengage, chat, and misbehave without remorse. The fix, he says, is not to care less but to redirect that care toward providing excellent instruction while fiercely protecting students' freedom to do their own work without interference. Teachers must stop coaxing, prodding, and shouldering responsibilities that belong to students. The article closes with the instruction to be warm while teaching but calm and still once students are working, leaving space for them to fill with their own motivation.
points: Caring too much about student outcomes is identified as a hidden trait that drives micromanagement in struggling teachers.
Micromanaging behaviors include over-helping, narrating, reminding, and constant check-ins, all of which increase teacher stress.
When a teacher absorbs too much responsibility for outcomes, students are left with no room to care about their own behavior or learning.
The remedy is not caring less, but redirecting care toward excellent instruction while protecting students' freedom to work independently.
Teachers should be warm and emotive while teaching, then calm and still while students work, leaving space for their own motivation.
quotes: The predominant teacher behavior associated with this trait is micromanagement. That is, they tend to over-help students by narrating, guiding, reminding, and talking them through just about everything.
But caring too much doesn’t just upset the balance of effective teaching and learning. It upends the apple cart. Because, when you care too much, you don’t leave room for your students to care .
Doing so severely weakens their motivation, work habits, and desire to behave.
Be warm, emotive, and enthusiastic while teaching lessons . But when it’s time for your students to do their part, be as calm and cool as a palm tree.
Move back and away, still and quiet, leaving a void for them to fill with their own passion, purpose, and determination.
